brief_data.hook:
"Make it more actionable." "Be more visible." You nod, guess, and find out too late.
Here is a one-sentence way to check what someone means, and why it's cheaper than guessing.
brief_data.summary: On Friday night Sena sends Mark a dashboard she spent a day on, and he replies that he meant "the other thing" by "actionable." She had been afraid to ask. Daniel shares Dingemanse and colleagues' 2015 study of about 48.5 hours of informal talk in twelve languages, where someone signaled "I didn't get that" about once every 1.4 minutes and people chose the most specific question they could, with honest limits about casual conversation. He tells the story of Imogen, a director who asked him to be "more visible" and wanted two minutes at an executive review, not a thirty-slide deck. Japan vs the US: "Yoroshiku onegaishimasu" and the secret second meeting in Tokyo, "Great question!" in Seattle, and the shared fear of asking a vice president. Today's challenge: when someone gives you a vague request, say "Just to make sure I understand, you want X by Y. Is that right?"
brief_data.thumb_cup: Say it back, ask if it's right
brief_data.thumb_sub: Check What They Mean in One Sentence

brief_data.hook:
The conversation moves faster than your courage. You wait for a gap, and the meeting moves on.
Here is a ten-second way to step in without stepping on anyone, and what research says about who hears an interruption.
brief_data.summary: At a Monday meeting in Tokyo with Laura in the room, Kato-san guesses "probably seasonal" about slide four while Ryo freezes, and Sena has about three seconds to step in. She waits for a gap that never comes, then asks Ryo, not the room, "Can I add something?" and explains in ten seconds that the April report and the new check count returned orders differently. Daniel shares Katherine Hilton's Stanford research on how American English listeners hear overlapping speech differently (500 listeners; a later survey of about 5,000 as reported by Stanford), with honest limits. He tells the story of Tobias, a VP who locked a launch date into the holiday code freeze while Daniel waited politely for a pause that never came. Japan vs the US: the soft "Sumimasen, hitotsu dake yoroshii deshou ka?" and aizuchi in Tokyo, the "quick add" flag in Seattle, and how Americans can open the door for Tokyo colleagues. Today's challenge: step in once with "Can I add something?", say one thing in about ten seconds, then hand it back.
brief_data.thumb_sub: Step Into a Conversation in Ten Seconds

brief_data.hook:
You have the answer ready, and so does everyone else. Before you give it, there is one sentence that shows you were listening.
Here is how to say someone's point back, with their reason, and what research says it does for how you are heard.
brief_data.summary: At a Monday lunch in Tokyo, Laura talks for four minutes about her worries over region three and then asks Sena what she thinks. Instead of giving five fixes, Sena takes a breath and says back the worry underneath, that nobody owns the word "ready," and asks "Did I get that right?" Daniel shares Yeomans, Minson and colleagues' 2020 study of conversational receptiveness (771 writers, 1,548 raters): replies that acknowledged understanding, found agreement and hedged were rated more receptive and a bit more persuasive, with honest limits about online strangers and political topics. He tells the story of Dmitri and Soraya, where his summary of a forty-minute debate was really his own view and cost the team three weeks. Japan vs the US: fukushou, repeating back, in Tokyo restaurants and phone calls, which checks facts but not worries, versus "What I'm hearing is..." in Seattle, which can sound like technique, and how Laura's "What did we decide?" summarizes the outcome but not the person. Today's challenge: before you give your opinion, say the other person's point with their reason in one sentence and ask "Did I get that right?"
thumb_notes: Ask: did I get that right?
brief_data.thumb_sub: Show You Heard Before You Disagree

brief_data.hook:
Someone says "Give me the quick version," and your whole month tries to come out at once. You have thirty seconds and fourteen pages.
Here is a three-sentence way to retell any meeting or project, and a simple test for what you actually remember.
brief_data.summary: Laura asks Sena for thirty seconds on region three at a leadership sync. The night before, Sena had read her fourteen pages six times and felt ready, but when she closed the notebook and retold the month from memory she couldn't say Wendell's date. Kato-san's hallway question, "what to worry about this week, and what to do about it," turns it into three sentences: where it stands, what could break, what I need. Daniel shares Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 testing-effect study (120 and 180 undergraduates): retelling from memory beat rereading after two days and a week even though rereading won at five minutes, with honest limits about students, short passages and written recall. He tells the story of Hector, a director who asked "Is the project late?" after Daniel saved the bad news for the end of a day-by-day update. Japan vs the US: "ketsuron kara itte" versus keii, the background that comes first in Tokyo emails, versus bottom line up front in many American companies, plus Laura's one-line "Bottom line?" and Kato-san's twelve-words-on-top fix. Today's challenge: after one meeting, close your notes and say the main point out loud in thirty seconds, record it, then check what you dropped and added.

brief_data.hook:
You are waiting to feel ready before you speak in the meeting, and the room keeps moving. Your heart is loud, and you are sure everyone can see it.
Here is why the first minute is the easiest time to speak, a one-sentence opener, and what research says about how nervous you really look.
brief_data.summary: Thursday's call has Mark's whole launch team, eleven people Sena has never met, and Laura wants her to open it. After a perfect three-paragraph opening that begins with an apology, Sena writes only one specific first sentence, rates her nerves in the margin (7 at midnight, 8 at 7:58), and opens with a line about marketing's banner. Her nerves go to 5 after the sentence and 3 by minute ten. Daniel shares Savitsky and Gilovich's 2003 illusion-of-transparency studies: 40 Cornell students rated themselves as looking more nervous (6.55) than their partners did (5.25), and speakers told about the illusion were rated more composed and gave better speeches than speakers who got nothing or plain reassurance (77 speakers), with honest limits, including a 2011 master's thesis with 31 anxious students that found no significant differences. He tells the story of Lucia, who said his on-call idea half-baked in minute three while he waited for his numbers. Japan vs the US: "Nanika goiken wa arimasu ka?" and a seven-second silence in Tokyo, where the meeting confirms and nemawashi does the thinking, versus "Strawman" and "half-baked, but..." in Seattle, and why "ready" means two different things. Today's challenge: say one sentence in the first minute of your next meeting and write your nerves, 1 to 10, before and after.
thumb_notes: Add one detail only you have
Say it in the first minute
brief_data.thumb_sub: Speak in the First Minute, Before You're Ready

brief_data.hook:
"No chart on slide one. Start with a person." Your director just said it, and you have fourteen pages of columns and nobody to point to.
Here is a four-part way to open any talk with one real person, and a test for whether your story is true enough to tell.
brief_data.summary: Laura wants three minutes from Sena at next Wednesday's Seattle product review: "No chart on slide one. Start with a person." Sena has fourteen pages and no person. Kato-san tells her to call Tanabe-san, an Osaka store manager who builds her weekly numbers by hand. At 7:40 a.m. Sena calls her; Tanabe-san says to use her name and tells her about Sunday nights: ninety minutes of copying six days of sales, and last Sunday at eleven she found she had typed Tuesday twice. Daniel shares Small, Loewenstein and Slovic's 2007 study: 159 people on a Pennsylvania campus each earned five dollars and could donate to Save the Children; Rokia, a seven-year-old girl, drew $2.38 on average against $1.14 for statistics, and a group that saw both gave $1.43. He is honest about the limits: a charity donation, students and passersby, and a 2024 pre-registered replication that found no support for the effect, so person-first is his judgment, not the paper's. He tells the story of Pilar, who asked "Whose ticket is that?" when he saved his customer for slide thirteen. Japan vs the US: Kato-san's Osaka deck puts the customer's voice last as "Customer A" to protect the person, while Laura asks "What's her name? What did she do last Tuesday?" The skill: open with one real person (a name, a place and a moment, one detail only they gave you, then your number), after checking you heard it from them, can say it in their words, and they agreed to be named. Last challenge recap, today's one-day challenge, and a cliffhanger: Mark asks for a region three view by Monday 9 a.m. Tokyo time.
thumb_notes: One detail only they gave you
brief_data.thumb_sub: Open Your Talk with One Real Person

brief_data.hook:
"Monday, 9 a.m. your time!!" Your draft reply is two words, "Yes, sure," and you've been staring at it for eleven hours.
Here is a three-part reply for a deadline you can't meet, and a quick way to guess how long something will really take.
brief_data.summary: Mark asks for a region three view by Monday 9 a.m. Tokyo time, three days of work, and Sena's draft reply is two words: "Yes, sure." She asks Kenta (region two took four days plus one to fix a filter) and Ryo (the Osaka script: two days planned, six taken), then shows Kato-san her reply: a one-page preview by Tuesday 9 a.m. her time, or the full view after Wednesday, and "Which would help more on Wednesday?" Mark answers in four seconds: "OH. One page!!" Daniel shares Buehler, Griffin and Ross's 1994 planning-fallacy study: 37 psychology students at the University of Waterloo predicted 33.9 days to finish their honors thesis and took 55.5; only 29.7% finished by their best guess and 10.8% by the optimistic date. He is honest about the limits (students, one big project, 1994; observers judging others guessed too long) and says only that your own guess is the one most likely to leave out the filter that breaks. His failure story: he told Odette two weeks for a data export that had taken five weeks before; it took thirty-four days, and Odette had already told her VP. Japan vs the US: Kato-san's "Kentou shimasu" (a polite no heard as yes) and "Nantoka shimasu" (a yes with a hidden cost) vs Laura's "What's the real deadline? What happens if it's Tuesday?", and Seattle's cheerful "Sure, no problem!" The skill: push back with an offer (what I can do and by when, what has to move, what matters most), after checking how long the last similar task took. Last challenge recap, today's one-day challenge, and a cliffhanger: Laura's three questions for Wednesday, the last of which nobody can answer, and "Please don't guess."
thumb_notes: What I can do, by when
brief_data.thumb_sub: Say No to the Date, Offer What You Can Do

brief_data.hook:
"Please don't guess." Your director's note ends there, and you're one question away from writing a number you made up.
Here is a three-part way to say "I don't know yet" without losing anyone's trust, and what two studies say about sounding sure.
brief_data.summary: Laura's note ends "Please don't guess," and Sena has been guessing for nine hours: at 4 a.m. she wrote "about thirty" stores in her notebook for question three, with no source. Kenta, on a Saturday morning, tells her the check log only sees stores that send a file; nineteen sent nothing in September and he can't tell why, then apologizes: "This isn't the answer." Ryo calls: "Please don't write thirty. Once a number's written down, somebody plans around it." Daniel shares two studies. Tenney, MacCoun, Spellman and Hastie (2007): in Experiment 1, 48 undergraduates read a mock trial summary; when the eyewitness was wrong, the confident one scored 4.6 out of 7 on credibility and the one who said he wasn't certain scored 5.2 (with no error, 5.7 vs 5.0). In Experiment 2, 103 undergraduates judged two car-accident witnesses: before any error 75.5% believed the sure one, after each was wrong about one small detail 58.4% believed the careful one. Gaertig and Simmons (2018): 11 studies, 4,806 people rating advice on sports, weather and stocks; "I'm not sure, but I think" was rated lower than confident advice, but "about a 57 percent chance" was not rated lower than flat certainty, and more than eight in ten chose the advisor who gave a chance. He gives the limits (strangers rating written descriptions, students and online panels, not workplaces; people may prefer certainty when they want to be persuaded) and says the conclusion that a wrong flat guess costs more than it saves is his judgment. Why AI can't: it offers "roughly thirty to forty percent" with no survey named, and isn't in the room on Wednesday. Daniel's failure story: Corinne, head of operations at his biggest customer, asked what percent of tickets are solved in one touch; he said "eighty percent" in six seconds, she put it on a slide for her CEO, and five weeks later the dashboard said sixty-one: "What else did you tell me that was a guess?" Japan vs the US: Kato-san's "Kakunin shimasu" to his division head with no date (the question returned three weeks later as "Re: Re: old report"; "a promise with no date") and why "Wakarimasen" can sound unprepared, vs Laura's "Is that a number or a guess?" and Hannah's "I don't know yet. I'll know Thursday at noon." The skill: say it plainly, say what you do know with a label (known, estimated or guess), say how and when you'll find out. Last challenge recap, today's one-day challenge, and a cliffhanger: Kato-san is in Osaka until Thursday and Laura wants Sena to run Tuesday's 9 a.m. prep call, eleven people, four items from Mark, no agenda, title "Sync."
brief_data.thumb_sub: Say I Don't Know Yet, Keep Their Trust
